problem: Standard RL for embodied agents (PointNav, Furniture Moving, Football) collapses when trained from only terminal rewards, so the field relies on hand-shaped rewards, experts or human annotation that do not scale to complex tasks.
motivation: Shaped rewards and experts are labor-intensive or infeasible for physics-based multi-agent tasks. The authors hypothesize the failure comes from learning perception and planning jointly, which makes learning non-stationary. Perfect-perception gridworlds should let an agent learn planning from terminal rewards.
key_idea: Train an agent with terminal rewards in a fast task-independent gridworld that mirrors the visual environment, then distill its policy into a visual agent by imitation learning (DAgger).
insight: Decoupling planning from perception is what makes terminal-reward learning work: DirectPix gets ~0 SPL on PointNav, while distillation from the gridworld expert reaches 63.8 SPL. The distilled agent is also sample-efficient (about 70% of final SPL within 5M steps). Distillation also improves shaped-reward training (GridToPix→DirectPix), so the gain is not only about avoiding reward shaping. The gridworld expert is a loose upper bound (78.8 SPL).
method: Terminal reward structure: reward is only a success reward (optionally time-decayed, alpha=0.9 for PointNav) with no goal-dependent progress term, and no step penalty except in Furniture Moving.

Gridworld mirrors: Grid-Habitat is an egocentric top-down occupancy+goal map; Grid-AI2-THOR is a 9-channel semantic top-down tensor; Grid-Google-Football is a 1D state vector of relative player, ball and goal positions.
Gridworld expert training: same architecture and RL algorithm (PPO/A3C) as the visual agent, with a minimally edited observation encoder, trained to near saturation on terminal rewards.

Policy distillation: the visual policy is trained with a cross-entropy loss to match the gridworld expert's action distribution given the visual history. Exploration is annealed teacher forcing (DAgger), and no gridworld is needed at test time.
GridToPix→DirectPix hybrid: IL warm start followed by RL fine-tuning of the visual agent.
Extra testbed: Visual Predator-Prey in MPE, where perfect reward shaping is intractable.

setting.backbone: CNN-GRU (PointNav, PPO), CNN-LSTM SYNC (Furniture Moving, A3C), CNN (Football, parallel PPO), all trained from scratch; the gridworld expert has the same architecture with a modified grid encoder
setting.training_data: No external data. Terminal-reward RL in the gridworld, then imitation of the gridworld expert in the visual environment (self-generated). Budgets: 50M steps PointNav, 500k episodes Furniture Moving, 8M steps Football.
setting.observation: Visual agent: egocentric RGB (256x256 for PointNav) plus goal vector. Gridworld expert: top-down occupancy/semantic tensor or 1D state vector.
setting.action_space: Discrete low-level actions (4 for PointNav, 13 per agent for Furniture Moving, football actions)
setting.simulator: Habitat (Gibson), AI2-THOR, Google Research Football, OpenAI MPE
setting.privileged: The gridworld expert uses privileged perfect-perception state (occupancy, semantics, positions) at training time only; none at test time.

numbers.backbone: CNN-GRU RGB agent distilled from gridworld expert

numbers_note: Furniture Moving, Football and MPE results are also reported but omitted because they are not among the canonical navigation benchmarks. PointNav numbers are on Gibson val (14 scenes).
results: With terminal rewards only, GridToPix raises PointNav SPL from 0.1 to 63.8 (success 0.2 to 81.8), Furniture Moving success from 0.8% to 24.6%, and Football game score from 0.07 to 0.63; DirectPix fails in all three. With shaped rewards, the hybrid improves over DirectPix (PointNav SPL 54.7→69.1). GridToPix also beats IL from optimal shortest-path actions on PointNav (SPL 68.7, success 76.7).
limitations: A gridworld mirror must be designed for each environment, which needs privileged state access and per-task encoder edits.
The visual agent is bounded by the gridworld expert and still falls well below it (e.g. Furniture Moving success 24.6% vs 56%).
Evaluated only with basic CNN-RNN architectures on three tasks (plus MPE), not against task-specific SOTA.
